title: SLO-aware stochastic gating for model rollouts
creator: Ana Patel
description:
Goal: Implement a policy compiler that translates high-level rollout intent (SLO targets, exposure budgets, cohort definitions, and safety constraints) into an executable release plan: a compact step schedule, per-step traffic splits (including stochastic gating fractions), shadow probes, and auto-rollback definitions.

Scope:
- Design a small declarative DSL for rollout intent: objectives (latency P90, error-rate, cost-per-token), exposure caps, cohort selectors, and acceptance tests.
- Compiler: convert intent to a time-ordered step schedule with deterministic initial fractions and a stochastic gate controller that can fuzz exposure to reduce correlated errors while preserving long-run fractions.
- Guardrails: synthesize metric-level thresholds (error-rate, latency, cost delta) and a cooldown/grace-mode for noisy signals.
- Runtime integration: enforcement hooks for the routing layer (traffic split tokens), shadow probe wiring, and an auto-rollback actuator.
- Observability: structured telemetry for each rollout step, decision reasons (why a step advanced/held/rolled back), and a simulation harness for offline verification.

Non-goals: full A/B experiment analytics (to be handled by experiments service), UI polish for rollout builder (console UX handled in a follow-up ticket).

Acceptance criteria:
- Policy compiler accepts DSL input and outputs a step schedule JSON and guardrail bundle.
- Runtime can read compiler output and enforce stochastic gating fractions with less than 5% allocation variance in steady state.
- Auto-rollback triggers when a configured guardrail breaches for 3 consecutive evaluation windows.
- Simulation test cover at least 5 synthetic failure modes (latency spike, increased 5xx, degraded quality signals, metric flapping, instrumentation gaps).

Rationale and trade-offs:
- Stochastic gating reduces correlated failure exposure for short-lived bursts versus deterministic fraction allocation, but adds variance; we balance by bounding per-window allocation and smoothing with a secondary deterministic floor.
- Compiler complexity vs runtime: we prefer a compact step plan and simple runtime enforcement over pushing complex logic into the router to keep rollback predictable across deployment modes (hosted/dedicated/private).

Design artifacts: PRD and design spec: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ML/SLO-aware+Stochastic+Gating+Compiler (internal).
